claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the starting condition is a homogeneous simple solid solution.
The starting CoCrFeNiTi alloy has no detectable nanoscale precipitates.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength but favorable plasticity and machinability.
The absence of nanoscale ordered precipitates is the primary cause of the alloy's relatively low hardness and strength.
Other high-entropy or multiphase alloy systems gain strength from nanoscale ordered precipitates or related nanoscale features.
Thermal aging between 600 and 700 °C for hours can induce nanoscale ordering or intermetallic precipitation in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The nanoscale ordered precipitates or intermetallic particles formed during aging will impede dislocation motion.
Precipitation-induced obstruction of dislocation motion will increase hardness and compressive strength.
Precipitation strengthening will reduce plasticity relative to the as-cast condition.
In the precipitate-free homogeneous matrix, relatively easy dislocation glide produces better plasticity and machinability but lower strength.
Aged equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have measurably higher hardness than the as-cast alloy.
Aged equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have measurably higher compressive strength than the as-cast alloy.
Aged equimolar CoCrFeNiTi will have lower plastic strain than the as-cast alloy.
TEM or atom-probe analysis after aging should reveal nanoscale precipitates absent from the as-cast state.
The proposed mechanism is limited to initially single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi and may not apply to off-equimolar or initially multiphase alloys.
The proposed behavior applies to compressive testing from 25 °C through 600 °C, provided oxidation or other degradation is avoided.
